reason: What the Level Studio assumes about pixels, written down where a check can read it. A number the code believes and nothing counts is a number that goes stale; these are recounted by `make art-validate` against the tree.

tile.nibble_order: high nibble is the left pixel

cram.levels_why: Three bits per channel give eight steps, and the hardware does not space them evenly. This is the eight-step ramp emulators use for normal intensity; `CRAM_LEVELS_LINEAR` in tile_graphics.py holds the even one for comparison. Either way index 0 is black and index 7 is full, so the choice changes how a preview looks and never what is written back.

uncompressed_art.shapes_why: A payload is normally a length word followed by that many bytes of tiles, because the DMA byte count travels with the art rather than with the mapping that points at it. Two payloads hold two such blocks back to back. Thirty-one carry no length word because the code that uploads them knows the size already. Nothing else occurs, and `make art-validate` fails if it starts to.

palettes.command_layout: destination byte, one less than the colour count, then that many CRAM words
palettes.format_why: Gfx_LoadPaletteCommand reads the two header bytes and copies count+1 words into both the active and the shadow buffer, so a command is 2 + 2*count bytes and a full palette is $82. The destination is a byte offset into the buffer because dest - $1D00 sign-extends to PaletteActiveBuffer; a destination of $62 is line three colour one, which is how a command leaves a line's transparent colour alone. Gfx_LoadMultiplePalettes plays CommonPaletteCommand first and then walks signed offsets relative to Gfx_LoadPalettePreservingSharedColor until it reads a zero, so a screen's colours are what a list leaves behind rather than anything stored whole.

sprite_mappings.static_layout: attribute word, size byte, link byte, signed Y byte, signed X byte
sprite_mappings.dynamic_layout: attribute word, size byte in bits 24-31 of a longword whose low 24 bits point at the art, signed Y byte, signed X byte
sprite_mappings.format_why: Sprite_RenderMapping reads six bytes a piece and Sprite_RenderDynamicMapping reads eight, the extra two because the art pointer travels inside the piece and is recorded as a DMA source. Bit 15 of the attribute word ends the mapping rather than setting priority; the rest of the word is exclusive-ored with the object's attributes and its tile index added to the object's base, so both the flips and the tile are relative. The size byte is an OAM size field, bits 2-3 one less than the width in tiles and bits 0-1 one less than the height, which the renderers read back out of the piece to mirror the X offset by the piece's own width. Two spellings name the same format: the frames of the shared combat animations are ...SpriteFrameNN and are mappings like any other, which only became visible once the animation scripts started naming them. The plural ...SpriteFrames is not: those are pointer tables and animation scripts, and each is listed in `excluded` with what it turned out to be.

sprite_mappings.unnamed_trailing_blocks_why: Each holds a second length-prefixed block that no symbol names. The piece pointing at the payload asks for exactly the first block, so the extraction, which cut on referenced addresses, swallowed a following piece nothing points at. The piece's own size byte is the authority on how much it draws.

stage_tilemaps.format_why: Tilemap_QueueColumnFromDescriptor splits a world position three ways and looks the answer up three times: X>>8 into a 32x32 coarse map of chunk indices, (X>>5)&7 into a chunk of 8x8 pattern indices, ((X>>3)&3)*2 into a pattern of 4x4 name-table words. lsl.w #6 on a coarse byte and lsl.w #5 on a chunk byte are what fix the 64- and 32-byte sizes. None of the three is in the cartridge as such: asset command 6, LoadCompressedToRAM, decompresses them into RAM at the addresses the sixteen-byte streaming descriptor names, and a stage reaches its lists through StageTableIndex and Stage_AssetLoaderOffsets. So a stage's background is the RAM its asset lists leave behind, played in order.

stage_rendering.name_word_layout: bit 15 priority, bits 13-14 palette line, bit 12 vertical flip, bit 11 horizontal flip, bits 0-10 tile
stage_rendering.why: A name-table word is a VDP word and absolute, unlike a sprite piece's attribute word, which is exclusive-ored against its object. VRAM comes from the same asset lists as the maps: command 7, LoadCompressedToVRAM, is plain LZSS and carries every stage's background art. Nine transfers in the tree use command 3 and the independently verified bit-token codec in src/rendering/tile_processing.s; no stage table index reaches them, but the renderer decodes them for frontend consumers. Five indices draw nothing: 20, 21 and 22 load only the shared asset list and bring no tilemap of their own, and 17 and 18 are the two whose planes the entry path cannot be replayed for, listed with their reasons under two_planes.planes_not_reproduced.

two_planes.why: The configuration record's two entry modes are byte offsets into tables of descriptor pointers, biased by four because Stage_UpdateGameplayEntry indexes them with -4(a0,d0.w). Mode 0 is a constant fill of one name-table word and reads no map. Bit 15 is not a mirror despite Tilemap_MirrorOffsetRowAndQueueScrollingRow's name: it does subi.w #$1000,d1 and reads the same maps $1000 pixels further down. Plane B moves at a quarter of plane A because Scroll_UpdateQuarterHorizontalPosition is asr.w #2, and starts from its own camera, so a flat picture of a whole stage can only be exact at the starting camera. The backdrop is register 7, $10, which is palette line one colour zero rather than the first colour of CRAM.

planes_not_reproduced.why: Plane A is empty at the starting camera and plane B's maps resolve to font tiles. Stage 18 drives its planes from Stage18_UpdateScrollAndRenderTilemap, which calls Tilemap_PopulateStage18UnqueuedColumn itself, so the entry mode describes only the first screen and replaying it statically shows something the game never shows.
The same, through the same routine: plane A entry mode $8008 and a plane B that the stage's own scroll code overrides.

two_planes.plane_b_suppressed_why: Plane B is left out where its descriptor names maps the stage never loads or its procedural route is explicitly not reproduced. Sharing plane A's source maps is not an exclusion: each plane has its own camera and VDP destination, and the bounded source viewport composites both. This retains shared-map planes 7B and 8B without claiming their later stage-specific scroll, sprite or raster behavior.

object_sprites.why: An object's 8(a5) holds a mapping or an animation script. Anim_ResolveTimedMappingFrame reads four-byte entries: a signed offset to a mapping and a duration; zero duration makes the offset a jump. A handler selects its resting script directly or through a state table. The Stage_VisualAssetLoaderOffsets route expands compact tile commands into VRAM transfers and RAM tile-base words, with each destination producing (destination >> 5) | $800. Enemy_SetupBehaviorSprite uses slot zero plus global priority; bird, circling, homing, phase-pattern, and wasp initializers use named RAM slots at offsets 6, 12, 4, 8, and 10. The stage 12 floater's state-zero initializer constructs attribute $8000 directly. Stage18_MovingPlatform chooses both its mapping and attribute through a StageTableIndex threshold; all 15 placements take the lower-index branch. The type-$48 initializer uses a fixed $C80 base and sets attribute bit 12 from spawn parameter bit 1, which Sys_SpawnObject copies to $5E(a5). Type-$12C clears parameter bit 15 and selects both animation and attribute from an eight-byte interleaved table. A placement is previewed only when its mapping and own base or parameter route are proved. Eighteen visual loaders also play an object palette command before the tile transfer.
object_sprites.handlers_without_a_sprite_why: The bounded resting-symbol resolver has no proved state-zero mapping for these handlers. Some are wave controllers, spawners, or terrain animators; this inventory does not infer that every listed object is invisible. Each remains a marker until its own dispatch and graphics route are proved.
object_sprites.handlers_without_a_tile_base_why: A mapping tile index is relative; a wrong base shows another enemy's art in the right shape. The preview accepts a source-proved immediate, the default SpawnedEnemyTileAttr[0] setup path, one of five proved family state-zero initializers with its loaded RAM slot, the stage 12 floater's constructed $8000 attribute, the type-$48 spawn-parameter branch, or the type-$12C interleaved selector table. Other handlers, stages without the required slot, or unproved parameter branches remain markers rather than guessed sprites.
